 Philip Rivers is returning to his alma mater, where he was a four-year starter at QB from 2000 to '03. Andy Lyons / ALLSPORTS 
 By Stewart Mandel Nov. 8, 2026 Updated Share article 390 Three years ago, Indiana president Pamela Whitten and athletic director Scott Dolson executed college football’s perfect coaching search. After conducting a study of successful programs nationally, they identified three key criteria for potential candidates: 1) He had to be a proven head coach who could bring his own staff. 2) He needed to have considerable recruiting experience. 3) He needed to have a history of developing quarterbacks.
 This led them to an under-the-radar candidate named Curt Cignetti.
 Advertisement
 It was an emphatic lesson for schools everywhere that making the right hire is far more important than making a splash.
 Unfortunately, no one ever heeds that lesson.
 I get why NC State hired Philip Rivers , and I get why Wolfpack fans are thrilled about it. I’d be too if I just spent 14 years watching Dave Doeren go 8-5.
 I hate to ruin their party, but Philip Rivers is not remotely qualified to be the head coach of a Power 4 program. Just like all the other guys before him a school talked itself into despite having zero college coaching experience — like that other NFL celebrity NC State’s own rival hired a couple of years ago.
 Truly, no one ever learns.
 Big Ten’s CFP Bids, 9-0 Survivors: Winners and Losers Ira Gorawara I tried in my mailbag and on X this week to talk NC State out of this. I spent much longer than I should have researching the history of major-college coaches who’d never previously coached in college. As best I can tell, the last one who turned out OK was the legendary Paul Brown, whom Ohio State hired straight from Massillon (Ohio) High School. In 1941.
 More recent names that fit the profile include Belichick (9-12 so far, including 4-9 in ACC play), UAB’s Trent Dilfer (9-21 from 2023 to ’25), UNLV’s Tony Sanchez (currently 29-61 at UNLV and New Mexico State) and North Texas’s Todd Dodge (6-37 from 2007 to ’10). Colorado’s Deion Sanders doesn’t count because he moved up from Jackson State of the Football Championship Subdivision, but he is the ultimate NFL celebrity coach. After making an initial splash, he is now 19-27 in four seasons.
 But of course, no one wants to hear any of that when one of the most famous alumni in their university’s history comes home to save the day. To NC State fans, Rivers is forever the quarterback who led their team to its only 10-win season this century and who went on to become an eight-time Pro Bowler over 17 seasons. Not the guy whose Alabama high school team just got knocked out in the first round of the Class 4A playoffs.
 As best I can tell, NC State’s case for Rivers is this:
 He has a great football mind.
 The Buffalo Bills interviewed him last year.
 Yes, he lacks experience, but he’ll hire a great staff.
 He’ll be able to raise a boatload of money for the Wolfpack’s roster.
 He’ll turn every quarterback (including his four-star son) into an All-American.
 All of that sounds great. But all of that is just a theory, with nothing tangible to support it.
 The job of a college head coach is hard . More so today than ever. And frankly, actual coaching is only a small part of it.
 Advertisement
 These are not the old days of staff consisting of a head coach, nine assistants and a couple of graduate assistants. Rivers is becoming the CEO of a massive operation. He will have to hire 40-50 people overnight, none of whom he’ll have previously worked with. Even a few bad hires — heck, even one bad coordinator hire — can torpedo a program.
 He will need to oversee a big budget. He will need to evaluate hundreds of recruits a year, having previously evaluated none. He will have to navigate the transfer portal, despite having no previous connection to almost anyone in it, and he will have to deal with sleazy agents constantly demanding raises for their clients. Yes, he will have a GM and a player personnel staff to help manage all of that, but the head coach is still the one accountable for all of those decisions.
 And almost none of Rivers’ career experience to this point is particularly relevant to any of that. Case in point: UNC believed Belichick’s experience with the salary cap and free agency would make him uniquely qualified for the new era of college football. Then Belichick got there and found out real quickly how little NFL roster acquisition has in common with college roster building. (That, and he hired the most reviled GM in the sport, but that’s another story.)
 I actually think NC State could have gotten the exact same excitement/fundraising bump it’s hoping for with Rivers by hiring him as the GM with top billing on the org chart. That’s what Stanford did in bringing back Andrew Luck. Then Rivers, in consultation with AD Boo Corrigan, could hire an experienced college coach with an existing staff and perhaps a core of players he can bring with him from his current team.
 Like Cignetti did at Indiana. Or Bob Chesney at UCLA. Or Eric Morris at Oklahoma State. Or Brent Brennan at Arizona. Or Willie Fritz at Houston. You get my point.
 Advertisement
 College athletics is a big, big business, which unfortunately many of its leaders still run like the owner of a fantasy football team. In what other business would a company hire a CEO who has never worked in management? Heck, in what other business would a company fire its top executive, then turn around and hire his replacement a couple of weeks later without conducting a thorough search? Based primarily on nostalgia?
 But college football is no normal business. There are no guiding principles, just misplaced exuberance.
 I end this column by saying: I hope I’m wrong. Philip Rivers turning NC State into a powerhouse would be an amazing story, and the Wolfpack’s long-suffering fan base should really get to enjoy something grander than the Gasparilla Bowl.
 All he has to do is become a once-every-85-years unicorn.
